q: Why can't the energy in glucose be used directly to power a membrane pump, without first being transferred to ATP?
options: Glucose cannot cross the plasma membrane, so its chemical energy is never available inside the cell
Glucose contains no chemical energy at all until mitochondria convert it into ATP molecules
Membrane pumps are driven by light energy absorbed by the membrane, which glucose can't supply
Glucose holds far too much energy for one pump; ATP delivers small packets by phosphorylating it
explanation: Cellular machinery is built to be driven by ATP: the terminal phosphate is transferred to the pump protein (phosphorylation), changing its shape. One mole of glucose holds ~2870 kJ – far more than any single reaction needs – so respiration 'repackages' it into ~30 ATP. This is why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.
